a: A diary that scrambles every word the instant you write it and unscrambles only for the right key.
e: An SED encrypts in the drive's own hardware, independent of the operating system.

a: A bouncer at the computer's front door who checks the OS's signature before letting it boot.
e: UEFI Secure Boot blocks unsigned bootloaders, stopping many rootkits and bootkits.

a: A mailroom inspector who opens every envelope, tosses scams and malware, and stops secrets going out.
e: An ESG is the enforcement point where SPF, DKIM and DMARC checks happen.

a: The heart of a single computer, turning wall current into the steady pulse components need.
e: A PSU powers one device; redundant PSUs remove a single point of failure.

a: A smart power strip for a whole server rack, often with per-outlet monitoring and control.
e: A PDU distributes power; it provides no backup unless fed by a UPS.

a: Splitting a book's pages between two couriers — twice as fast, but lose one courier and the book is gone.
e: RAID 0 offers zero fault tolerance; one failed drive destroys all data.

a: Writing every page in two identical notebooks — if one is lost, the other is complete.
e: RAID 1 survives one drive failure but halves usable capacity.

a: Three friends each hold part of a puzzle plus a checksum, so any one can rebuild a missing piece.
e: RAID 5 needs 3+ drives and survives exactly one failure.

a: The puzzle-sharing friends keep two checksums, so even losing two of them doesn't sink the puzzle.
e: RAID 6 needs 4+ drives and survives two simultaneous drive failures.

a: Two pairs of twin notebooks with the pages split between pairs — fast and fault tolerant.
e: RAID 10 needs 4+ drives and gives speed plus redundancy at 50% capacity.

a: A fully furnished, stocked spare office with the lights already on — move in within minutes.
e: A hot site meets the shortest RTO but is the most expensive option.

a: A spare office with desks and phones installed, but you still need to bring the files.
e: A warm site balances cost and recovery time, typically hours to days.

a: An empty rented warehouse with power and network jacks, waiting for you to furnish it.
e: A cold site is cheapest but takes days or weeks to activate.

a: A conductor who must hit every beat exactly on time — late is as bad as wrong.
e: An RTOS guarantees response deadlines, so heavy security tooling can be hard to add.

a: Rearranging a building's room numbers every morning so a burglar's floor plan is always wrong.
e: ASLR makes memory-corruption exploits unreliable by hiding where code and data live.

a: A robotic auditor reading a standard checklist and scanning every machine against it automatically.
e: SCAP standardizes formats like CVE and CVSS so scanners share the same language.

a: An air-traffic tower directing every plane centrally, instead of each pilot choosing routes alone.
e: SDN separates the control plane from switches, so the controller must be well protected.

a: A smart GPS for company traffic, picking the best internet or MPLS link for each app in real time.
e: SD-WAN optimizes and steers WAN traffic; it is not a security stack alone.

a: Renting a firewall in the cloud like a streaming subscription instead of buying a box for every office.
e: FWaaS protects remote users and branches without on-site firewall hardware.

a: Renting a fully equipped kitchen: you bring the recipe, they maintain the ovens.
e: In PaaS you own your code and data; the provider runs OS and runtime.

a: Moving the whole security checkpoint into the cloud so it follows every user wherever they work.
e: SASE bundles networking and security as one cloud service near the user.

a: The plan for keeping the restaurant serving customers when the kitchen floods.
e: BCP keeps the whole business running; DRP focuses on restoring IT.

a: The step-by-step guide for rebuilding the kitchen after the flood.
e: A DRP restores technology; the BCP keeps business functions alive meanwhile.

a: How far back the last save point is — lose power now, and you redo everything since then.
e: RPO is measured backward in data lost; RTO is measured forward in downtime.

a: The stopwatch that starts when the lights go out and must not run past the deadline.
e: RTO is how fast you must recover; RPO is how much data you can lose.

a: The steering wheel, the risk map, and the rulebook — making security serve the business and the law.
e: GRC aligns security decisions with business goals and regulatory obligations.

a: The blueprint process for building a house, from sketches to inspection to move-in.
e: The SDLC methodology structures development; SDLS embeds security into it.

a: Having the building inspector check every stage of construction, not just the finished house.
e: Fixing flaws during design costs far less than patching them after release.

a: Building a quick cardboard model, showing the client, and reshaping it again the same week.
e: RAD favors speed and prototypes, so security reviews must keep pace with iterations.

a: Anything that could point a stranger straight to your front door — name, SSN, face, address.
e: PII is any identifying data; PHI is the health-related subset.

a: Your medical chart — anything linking your name to your diagnosis or treatment.
e: PHI is health data linked to an identity and regulated under HIPAA in the US.

a: Europe's privacy rulebook that follows EU residents' data wherever in the world it travels.
e: GDPR applies to any organization processing EU residents' data, with heavy fines.

a: The US rulebook that keeps your doctor's files locked and tells clinics how to share them.
e: HIPAA governs US healthcare providers, insurers and their business associates.

a: The national cookbook of security recipes that much of the industry follows.
e: NIST publishes the CSF and SP 800 series; it is a US federal agency.

a: A contractor's job sheet listing exactly what gets built, by when, and what done looks like.
e: An SOW details one project under the broader terms of an MSA.

a: The government's plan to keep essential services running even if headquarters is unusable.
e: COOP is the government term for continuity planning of essential functions.

a: The average lifespan of a light bulb you'll throw away, not fix, when it dies.
e: MTTF applies to items replaced, not repaired, after failing.

a: The average time the mechanic needs to get your car back on the road.
e: Lower MTTR means faster recovery and helps meet the RTO.

a: How many miles your car usually drives between trips to the repair shop.
e: Higher MTBF means more reliable repairable systems.

a: A handshake on paper: both sides agree on intentions, but no court will enforce it.
e: An MOU signals cooperation without legal obligations, unlike an SLA or BPA.

a: How many times a year you expect the basement to flood.
e: ARO is a frequency, e.g. 0.5 for once every two years.

a: The yearly flood budget: what one flood costs multiplied by how often floods happen.
e: ALE = SLE × ARO; spending more than ALE on a control rarely makes sense.

a: The repair bill from one single basement flood.
e: SLE = AV × EF, the loss from one occurrence.

a: The price tag on what's at risk before anything bad happens.
e: AV is the starting point of quantitative risk math: SLE = AV × EF.

a: The formal partnership contract spelling out who invests, who decides, and how profits split.
e: A BPA defines the partnership itself, including roles, profits and responsibilities.

a: The umbrella contract signed once, so each new project needs only a short SOW.
e: An MSA sets general terms once; SOWs then define each project.

a: Checking a concert ticket at the gate, then someone swaps it before the scanner reads it.
e: TOCTOU exploits the gap after a check; atomic operations and locking close it.
m: Time Of Check Then Others Use

a: A pizza promise: delivered in 30 minutes or there's a penalty.
e: An SLA defines measurable uptime and response targets with penalties if missed.

a: Asking each department: if your systems vanished today, what would it cost and how fast must they return?
e: The BIA identifies critical functions and sets RTO and RPO for continuity plans.

a: The international recipe book, with ISO 27001 being the certifiable recipe for an ISMS.
e: ISO 27001 can be certified; ISO 27002 provides the control guidance.

a: How much of the house a single fire actually burns — 30% of it, say.
e: EF is a percentage of asset value lost in one incident.

a: The rulebook telling US banks and lenders to keep your financial details under lock.
e: GLBA applies to US financial institutions and requires a written security program.

a: The long legal fine print you scroll past and accept before installing an app.
e: A EULA is the vendor's contract with users; an AUP is the employer's policy.

a: The house rules every employee signs: what you may and may not do with company tech.
e: An AUP sets user behavior expectations and supports disciplinary action.
